economics: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote that a good economist always looks at both what is seen and what is unseen. In 2005 the US Renewable Fuel Standard required refiners to blend corn ethanol into gasoline. American farmers responded by moving huge fields out of food crops and into fuel corn. Bastiat's rule says the food that never got grown is what?

Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by an anonymous programmer known only as Satoshi Nakamoto. A whole bitcoin can be split into one hundred million tiny units, and those tiny units were named in his honor so his contribution would live on inside the currency. What is this smallest denomination called?
history: In the summer of 1665 a deadly outbreak — the Great Plague of London — swept across England, killing about a quarter of London's people. To keep students from carrying the sickness home, Cambridge University shut its doors. A 22-year-old student named Isaac Newton went home to the family farm at Woolsthorpe and stayed there for nearly two years — the famous 'wonder years' when he first worked out gravity and calculus. What disease had closed the university?
theology: Brynhild boasted that only Gunnar had crossed the ring of fire. Gudrun laughed at her claim, and said Sigurd had crossed the fire wearing Gunnar's face. To prove the story, Gudrun held up a single object Sigurd had taken from Brynhild that night. What did Gudrun hold up as her proof?

In ancient Greek myth, the proud hunter Narcissus wasted away by a still pool in Boeotia, unable to stop staring at his own reflection. The wood-nymphs and the mountain-echo Echo mourned him and came for the boy's body to burn it on a pyre. But where he had lain by the water they found no body at all -- only a small flower with white petals and a golden centre, growing at the edge of the pool. What is that flower still called?
trivia: In 2006 Nintendo released a small white home console that came with a slim wand-shaped controller. Sensors on top of the TV read the wand's motion, so players swung it in the air to hit tennis balls, bowl strikes, and throw punches in the pack-in game Wii Sports. Grandparents and little kids picked it up as easily as teenage gamers, and the machine sold out worldwide for months. Name the system.
